name: TPA3251D2DDVR
title: TPA3251: 175 W stereo / 350 W mono analog-input class-D amplifier, HTSSOP-44
summary: The TPA3251 is a four-half-bridge class-D power amplifier with differential analog inputs, a fixed inverting gain of 20 dB and closed-loop feedback that includes the gate drivers. From a 12 V to 38 V power rail plus a 12 V gate and logic rail it drives two bridged channels (175 W into 4 Ω at 10 % THD+N), one paralleled channel (350 W into 2 Ω), four single-ended channels or a 2.1 mix. Its 60 mΩ output FETs keep power-stage idle loss below 1 W, and it guards itself against undervoltage, overtemperature, overcurrent, DC on the speaker and shorted output pins, reporting on two open-drain flags.

circuits.title: Stereo BTL, differential inputs
circuits.description: Two bridged channels, mode 00 (M1 and M2 grounded). Each of the four inputs comes in through a 10 µF coupling capacitor. VDD sits on the 12 V rail with 470 µF and 100 nF; each gate-drive pin is fed from that rail through its own 3.3 Ω resistor with 100 nF to ground. OC_ADJ has 22 kΩ to ground (CB3C, about 16.3 A) and FREQ_ADJ 10 kΩ (nominal 600 kHz, master). DVDD and AVDD each take 1 µF, VBG 100 nF and C_START 10 nF. The PVDD rail has four 1 µF ceramics and two 470 µF bulk capacitors at the supply pins. Each output has a 33 nF bootstrap capacitor from its BST pin and a 10 µH inductor; after each inductor are 1 µF, 1 nF and a 10 nF + 3.3 Ω snubber, all to ground, and the speaker sits between the A and B (or C and D) filter outputs. OSC_IOM and OSC_IOP are left open.

circuits.title: Four single-ended channels
circuits.description: Four SE channels, mode 11: M1 and M2 are tied to DVDD. Supply, input and programming parts match the BTL circuit except C_START, which takes 470 nF. Each output runs through a 15 µH inductor to a node with 1 µF, 1 nF and a 10 nF + 3.3 Ω snubber to ground, then through a 470 µF capacitor (positive side at the filter) to a speaker whose other end is grounded.
notes: The SE design requirements give the output filter as 15 µH + 680 nF; this circuit carries 1 µF.

circuits.title: Mono PBTL, differential input
circuits.description: One paralleled bridge, mode 10: M1 grounded, M2 on DVDD, INPUT_C and INPUT_D grounded, and the signal on INPUT_A and INPUT_B through 10 µF each. Supply and programming parts match the BTL circuit. After the four 10 µH inductors, OUT_A and OUT_C join on one side of the speaker and OUT_B and OUT_D on the other; each side has 680 nF, 1 nF and a 10 nF + 3.3 Ω snubber to ground.
notes: The PBTL design requirements give the output filter as 10 µH + 1 µF; this circuit carries 680 nF.

operation.text: Two rails run the part: PVDD (12 V to 38 V, 36 V typical) for the output stages and one 12 V rail for GVDD_AB, GVDD_CD and VDD. Internal regulators make AVDD and DVDD from VDD; they serve only the part's own circuits and carry no outside load. The three 12 V pins are best split from one another on the board with RC filters, and every decoupling capacitor goes close to its pin with a small loop to the GND pins. Both rails should be quiet and low in impedance.

The four half-bridges are identical and independent, each with its own BST pin; PVDD and GVDD are split per full bridge (AB and CD). A ceramic capacitor from each BST pin to its OUT pin is charged through an internal diode from GVDD while the output is low, then rides above the output to supply the high-side driver. 33 nF in 0603 or 0805 holds enough charge to keep the high-side FET on through the shortest PWM duty cycles.

Each PVDD pin group needs a 1 µF ceramic placed as close to the pins as it will go; this matters for performance, EMI and reliability. Those 1 µF parts see the PWM overshoot, heat and ripple current, so X7R with at least a 50 V rating is called for on a 36 V supply. The bulk PVDD capacitors want low ESR; 1000 µF, 50 V covers most designs with a sound supply.

No supply order is needed: a power-on reset circuit and protection against parasitic gate charging make the ramp rates uncritical. Holding RESET low for at least 400 ms after PVDD comes up keeps start-up quiet. The outputs stay high impedance until GVDD and VDD pass the UVP threshold.

Releasing RESET pulls FAULT low and enables the AVDD regulator; AVDD ramps in about 100 µs and FAULT rises when it passes its UVP threshold. A precharge of about 220 ms then settles the DC level on the input coupling capacitors before the output ramp starts, timed by the C_START capacitor. In BTL modes, RESET low turns on a weak pulldown of each output so the bootstrap capacitors are charged before switching begins.
No power-down order is needed; the part keeps working while GVDD and VDD stay above UVP. Pulling RESET low before the supplies fall gives a controlled ramp-down and avoids pops.

The amplifier inverts: the output is the inverse of the input, with a gain of 20 dB. Inputs are differential (2N) in BTL and PBTL and single-ended (1N) in SE; the example designs allow ±3.9 V peak on each input, and the input resistance is 24 kΩ.
M1 and M2 pick stereo BTL (00), 2.1 with one BTL and two SE outputs (01), mono PBTL (10, INPUT_C and INPUT_D grounded) or four SE outputs (11).

FAULT and CLIP_OTW are active-low open-drain outputs, each with an internal pullup of about 26 kΩ to the 3.3 V DVDD. FAULT goes low on any shutdown fault; CLIP_OTW goes low when the junction passes 125 °C and also signals that the output is nearing clipping. Holding RESET low forces FAULT high whatever the fault state. A controller watching CLIP_OTW can turn the volume down before an overtemperature shutdown, or a tracking supply can step up to a higher rail.

On a fault the power stage goes high impedance and FAULT is pulled low. Undervoltage faults clear themselves once the supply recovers; overload and overtemperature errors stay latched until RESET is cycled.

Every high-side and low-side FET has a fast current sensor with a resistor-set threshold. In cycle-by-cycle mode (CB3C, OC_ADJ 22 kΩ to 30 kΩ) an overcurrent flips that half-bridge's state until the next PWM frame begins, so music peaks into a dipping speaker impedance pass without a shutdown. An overload counter counts up on each overcurrent frame and down on each clean one; if it reaches its limit (1.7 ms at 600 kHz) the channel shuts down, high impedance, until RESET is cycled. In latched mode (OC_ADJ 47 kΩ to 64 kΩ) the first overcurrent shuts the channel down at once. A resistor outside both ranges gives the minimum threshold.

In BTL mode the part compares the current into and out of each bridged output; an imbalance past 1.5 A, such as a speaker lead shorted to chassis that puts PVDD/2 across the speaker, runs the overload counter up and shuts the channel. The check is off in PBTL and SE modes.

At start-up, when VDD arrives, the part first checks every OUT pin for a short to GND and then for a short to PVDD, right at the pins ahead of the filter; a short appearing later is not caught by this test. While it runs FAULT stays low and RESET is ignored; a short holds all half-bridges in high impedance until it is removed, and then start-up carries on. The test time scales with the LC filter capacitance, under 15 ms per µF. A reset does not repeat it. It runs in BTL and PBTL but not in SE, and a resistive load from an output to GND or PVDD can trip it.

CLIP_OTW goes low above 125 °C junction (typical). Above 155 °C every half-bridge goes high impedance and FAULT goes low; this state is latched and cleared by asserting RESET. RESET should only be released once CLIP_OTW is high again, and its rising edge should come at least 4 ms after FAULT falls.

GVDD_X and VDD are monitored separately; if any falls below the UVP threshold (9.5 V typical) all outputs go high impedance and FAULT goes low, and operation resumes by itself once every supply is back above it. Power-on reset clears the overload circuit at start-up. A bootstrap capacitor undervoltage stops only its half-bridge, without FAULT, until the capacitor recharges.

A global fault stops all PWM activity and pulls FAULT low; a channel fault stops only the affected channels. In slave mode, losing the OSC_IO clock (below the minimum frequency) puts the outputs in high impedance until the clock returns.

RESET low ramps the outputs down and then turns the FETs off (high impedance); the output pulldowns are on with RESET low in both SE and BTL modes. A rising edge on RESET restarts the part after an overload fault and runs the start-up sequence.

In master mode a resistor from FREQ_ADJ to GND sets the PWM frame rate: 10 kΩ for 600 kHz, 20 kΩ for 500 kHz (AM1) and 30 kΩ for 450 kHz (AM2). The lower settings exist to move switching harmonics away from an AM receiver's tuned station; the pair of frequencies is chosen to leave the fewest clashes across the band.

Pulling FREQ_ADJ to DVDD stops the internal oscillator and turns OSC_IOP and OSC_IOM into inputs for a differential clock from a master. The slave's switching is then offset from the master's so no two idle channels switch together, which eases supply noise without touching the audio. Wiring the OSC_IO pair with the same polarity (+ to +) selects slave mode 1; crossing it (+ to -) selects slave mode 2.

Ordinary audio analysers misread class-D outputs because of the out-of-band switching residue. The figures use AES17 plus AUX-0025 pre-filters; failing those, a 30 kHz low-pass of 10 Ω and 47 nF on the output does the job.

The HTSSOP package carries its heat slug on the top face, meant for a heat sink, and the sink must be grounded. The GND pins are the best thermal conductors on the board side, so the ground copper should run unbroken from them into the area around the part.
FR-4 with 2 oz (70 µm) copper is recommended; it allows more output power, runs cooler and gives better EMI margin through lower trace inductance.

Use one unbroken ground plane as the return for power and audio, and keep a solid local ground under the part. Run each audio input short and alongside its source ground. Put the small PVDD bypass capacitors right at the PVDD pins, under the heat sink, and the bulk PVDD capacitors as near the PVDD and GND pins as the heat sink allows, on wide top-layer traces with no vias in the current path. Point the narrow end of each passive toward the part unless copper can flow between its pads, keep other hot parts away, and do not cut the heat path from the part into the ground copper with traces or via rows, above all on the output side. Unused board area is ground pour.
